t.1.2.1: The seers said: O son of the Sūta, that which you spoke of as Samantapañcaka, all of this we wish to hear in its proper order.
t.1.2.2: The bard said: If you have the desire, O brahmins, then, O best of the virtuous, you should listen to me as I tell auspicious stories, and to the account of the place called Samantapañcaka.
t.1.2.3: At the juncture of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, Rāma, the best of those who bear weapons, driven by indignation, repeatedly slew the royal kṣatriya order.
t.1.2.4: He, radiant as fire, having destroyed the entire warrior class by his own might, made five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.
t.1.2.5: In those lakes whose waters were blood, he, overwhelmed by wrath, satisfied his ancestors with blood; thus have we heard.
t.1.2.7: The region that lies near those lakes whose waters are blood is proclaimed to be the holy Samantapañcaka.
t.1.2.6: Then the ancestors, led by Ṛcīka, approached that bull among brahmins and restrained him, saying, “Forgive!” And so he desisted.
t.1.2.8: By whatever distinguishing mark a region is observed to be characterized, by that very name, the wise say, that region should be called.
t.1.2.9: And when the interval between the Kali and Dvāpara ages had arrived, the battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas took place at Samantapañcaka.
t.1.2.10: In that supremely righteous land, free from any defect of the earth, eighteen akṣauhiṇīs assembled with the desire to fight.
t.1.2.11: Thus, O twice-born ones, did the name of that region come about. That region, holy and delightful, has been described to you.
t.1.2.12: All this I have told you, O best of sages: how that region became famed, renowned throughout the three worlds.
t.1.2.13: The sages said: O son of the Sūta, that which you have spoken of as "akṣauhiṇīs", all of this we wish to hear exactly as it is.
t.1.2.14: Tell us also, exactly as it is, the measure of an akṣauhiṇī in chariots, horses, men and elephants, for everything is known to you.
t.1.2.15: One chariot and one elephant, five men on foot, and three horses: this, by those who know it, is called a patti.
t.1.2.16: The wise call this patti, when tripled, a senāmukha; three senāmukhas together are called one gulma.
t.1.2.17: Three gulmas make what is called a gaṇa, and three gaṇas a vāhinī; three vāhinīs, in turn, are known by the wise as a pṛtanā.
t.1.2.18: Three pṛtanās make a camū, and three camūs make an anīkinī; an anīkinī multiplied tenfold the wise call an akṣauhiṇī.
t.1.2.19: O best of the twice-born, those who know the true principles of number and calculation reckon the chariots of an akṣauhiṇī at twenty-one thousand.
t.1.2.20: And eight hundreds above that, and seventy more besides: this indeed one should declare here as the number of the elephants.
t.1.2.21: Of men too, O sinless ones, the number should be known as one hundred thousand and likewise nine thousand, and three hundred and fifty.
t.1.2.22: Likewise, they say that the horses number sixty-five thousand and six hundred plus ten, reckoned here exactly by count.
t.1.2.23: This, which I have described to you in detail, O best of the twice-born, is what people who know the true principles of numbers call an akṣauhiṇī.
t.1.2.24: By this reckoning, O best of the twice-born, there were akṣauhiṇīs in the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, and these, taken together, were eighteen in all.
t.1.2.26: Bhīṣma, knower of the supreme weapons, fought for ten days indeed; Droṇa, for his part, protected the army of the Kurus for five days.
t.1.2.25: Having assembled in that very region, the armies met their end right there, for Time, whose deeds are wondrous, made the Kauravas the cause.
t.1.2.27: Karṇa, the tormentor of enemy forces, fought for two days, while Śalya lasted half a day; after that came the battle with maces.
t.1.2.28: But at the end of that very day, Hārdikya, Drauṇi and Gautama slew in the night the army of Yudhiṣṭhira as it lay asleep, trusting and unsuspecting.
t.1.2.30: This narrative, with its varied meanings and words and its many conventions and doctrines, has been embraced by wise men, just as detachment is embraced by those who seek liberation.
t.1.2.29: As for the full narrative of the Bhārata told at the sacrificial session of Śaunaka, I shall relate it to you: in it comes, from the beginning, the tale of Pauloma and what follows after.
t.1.2.31: Like the self among the things that are to be known, and like life among things held dear, this itihāsa, whose purpose is supreme, is the best among all the sacred traditions.
t.1.2.33: Let the summary of the books be heard of this Bhārata history, attained through wisdom, whose books are made of wondrous words.
t.1.2.32: For in this supreme history the highest wisdom has been set down, just as the whole of speech, resting on the world and the Veda, is set in vowels and consonants.
t.1.2.34: First comes the Parvānukramaṇī, the Table of Contents of the Books, and second the Parvasaṃgraha, the Summary of the Books; then the Pauṣya, the Pauloma, the Āstīka, and the Ādivaṃśāvatāraṇa, the Descent of the First Lineages.
t.1.2.35: Then the Sambhava Parva is told, wondrous and fashioned by the gods; here too the burning of the lacquer house, and the Haiḍimba Parva is recited.
t.1.2.36: Then comes the Parvan of the Slaying of Baka, and after that the Caitraratha Parvan; then is declared the Parvan of the Svayaṃvara of the queen, the Pāñcāla princess.
t.1.2.38: Arjuna's dwelling in the forest, then the Abduction of Subhadrā; after the Abduction of Subhadrā should be known the Bringing of the Bridal Gifts.
t.1.2.37: Then, after the conquest won by the law of the kṣatriyas, comes what is remembered as the Vaivāhika; they know the parvan called Āgamana, and likewise the Rājyalambha.
t.1.2.39: Then comes the section called the Burning of the Khāṇḍava Forest, and right there the Encounter with Maya; after that the Sabhāparvan is declared, and beyond that the Mantraparvan.
t.1.2.40: The Slaying of Jarāsaṃdha is a parva, and likewise the Conquest of the Quarters is a parva; the parva after the Conquest of the Quarters is called the Rājasūyika.
t.1.2.41: And then the Bringing of the Guest-Offering, and after that the Slaying of Śiśupāla; then is declared the Book of the Dicing, and after this the Sequel to the Dicing.
t.1.2.42: Then comes the Book of the Forest, and also the Slaying of Kirmīra, and the battle between Īśvara and Arjuna, the book called Kairāta.
t.1.2.43: After this, the section called the Journey to Indra's World is to be known; then the section on the Pilgrimage to the Sacred Fords of the wise king of the Kurus.
t.1.2.44: The section on the slaying of Jaṭāsura, and after that the Battle with the Yakṣas; likewise, the section of the Serpent is to be known as following next.
t.1.2.46: Then comes the Parvan of the Ghoṣayātrā, then the Fear Caused by the Dream of the Deer; after that is told the tale of the Vrīhidrauṇika.
t.1.2.45: Immediately after that is declared the book of the Session with Mārkaṇḍeya, and then the book of the Dialogue between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā.
t.1.2.47: Then comes the section of the Abduction of Draupadī from the forest by the Saindhava; after that, the section of the Taking of the Earrings is told here.
t.1.2.48: Then the Parvan of the Fire-Sticks, and immediately after that the Parvan of Virāṭa; the Parvan of the Slaying of the Kīcakas, and then the Parvan of the Cattle-Raid.
t.1.2.49: The section on the marriage of Vairāṭī with Abhimanyu is remembered as the Vaivāhika Parva; after that, the most wondrous Udyogaparva is to be known.
t.1.2.50: Then, after this, should be known the parvan called the Journey of Saṃjaya; then the parvan of Prajāgara, the Night Vigil, owing to the anxiety of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.2.51: And the Parvan of Sanatsujāta, the secret vision of the supreme self; then the Yānasaṃdhi Parvan, and also the Parvan of the Blessed One's Journey.
t.1.2.52: Here should be known the Book of the Dispute, concerning the great-souled Karṇa as well; and after that the Book of the Marching Forth of the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.2.54: And after this, the Book of the Tale of Ambā is to be known; then the Book of the Consecration of Bhīṣma is to be known, wondrous in its cause.
t.1.2.53: The Book of the Counting of Chariot-Warriors and Great Chariot-Warriors is told, and right after it the Book of the Coming of Ulūka as Envoy, which heightens indignation.
t.1.2.55: Immediately after that is declared the parvan of the Construction of Jambūkhaṇḍa; then is to be known the Bhūmiparvan, the detailed account of the continents.
t.1.2.56: The Bhagavadgītā is declared a parvan, then the parvan of the slaying of Bhīṣma; the consecration of Droṇa is declared a parvan, then the slaying of the Saṃśaptakas.
t.1.2.57: The book of the Slaying of Abhimanyu and the book of the Vow are told; then the book of the Slaying of Jayadratha, and after that the Slaying of Ghaṭotkaca.
t.1.2.58: Then the Book of the Slaying of Droṇa is to be known, which makes the hair stand on end; the book that follows immediately after is called the Release of the Nārāyaṇa Weapon.
t.1.2.59: Then the Karṇaparvan is to be known, and after that the Śalyaparvan; then the Parvan of the Entering into the Lake, and after this the Club Fight.
t.1.2.60: Then comes the Sārasvata Parva, endowed with the merits of the lineage of the sacred fords; and after this the gruesome Sauptika Parva is told.
t.1.2.61: After that is set forth the most dreadful Aiṣīka Parva; then comes the Jalapradānika Parva, and after that the Strī Parva.
t.1.2.62: Next is to be known the Śrāddha Parvan, concerning the funeral rites of the Kurus, and then the Parvan of the consecration of the wise Dharmarāja.
t.1.2.63: Then comes the section on the subduing of Cārvāka, the demon in the guise of a brahmin; and immediately after that is declared the section on the apportioning of the dwellings.
t.1.2.64: Then comes the Śāntiparva, in which there is the recounting of the duties of kings, and the parva called Āpaddharma is declared; after that comes the Mokṣadharma.
t.1.2.65: Then should be known the excellent Ānuśāsanika Parva, the Book of Instruction; after that, the Svargārohaṇika Parva of the wise Bhīṣma, the book of his ascent to heaven.
t.1.2.66: Then comes the Āśvamedhika Parva, which destroys all sins; after that, the Anugītā Parva should be known, which speaks of the supreme self.
t.1.2.67: And the book called the Dwelling in the Hermitage, and the Seeing of the Sons, and after that the book of the Coming of Nārada are told here.
t.1.2.68: And after that the terrible Mausala Parva is described, then the Mahāprasthānika Parva, and after that the Svargārohaṇika Parva.
t.1.2.69: Then comes the Harivaṃśa, the parvan that is an ancient Purāṇa called the Khila; and the Bhaviṣyat-parvan is also declared among the Khilas, great and wondrous.
t.1.2.71: In the Naimiṣa forest the eighteen parvans were indeed recounted. This is the summary of the Bhārata, the compendium of the parvans that was told there.
t.1.2.70: These full hundred books were proclaimed by the great-souled Vyāsa, and then recited again, faithfully and in due order, by the son of the sūta Lomaharṣaṇa.
t.1.2.72: In the Pauṣya section the greatness of Uttaṅka is described; in the Pauloma section the extent of the lineage of Bhṛgu is recounted.
t.1.2.73: In the Āstīka section are told the origin of all the serpents and of Garuḍa, the churning of the Ocean of Milk, and likewise the birth of Uccaiḥśravas.
t.1.2.74: This tale of the great-souled Bhāratas came forth while King Pārikṣita was performing sacrifice by means of the snake sacrifice.
t.1.2.75: In the Sambhavaparvan are told the various births of kings, and also of other brahmins, and of the seer Dvaipāyana.
t.1.2.76: And here is recounted the descent in partial incarnations of the gods, of the Daityas and the Dānavas, and of the Yakṣas of great might.
t.1.2.77: Then the origin of the Nāgas and the serpents, of the Gandharvas and the birds, and of various other beings as well.
t.1.2.78: The rebirth of the great-souled Vasus from Bhāgīrathī in the house of Śaṃtanu, and their ascent once more to heaven.
t.1.2.79: Here too is told the birth of Bhīṣma from the union of portions of splendour, his turning away from the kingdom, and his steadfastness in the vow of celibacy.
t.1.2.80: The keeping of his vow, and the protection of Citrāṅgada; and, when Citrāṅgada had been slain, the protection of his younger brother.
t.1.2.81: Likewise, the installation of Vicitravīrya in the kingship, and the birth of Dharma among men, which sprang from the curse of Aṇīmāṇḍavya.
t.1.2.82: And the birth, arising from a granted boon, of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, and the origin of the Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.2.83: The journey to Vāraṇāvata, and the plot of Duryodhana, and, at the word of Vidura, the undertaking of the digging of a tunnel.
t.1.2.84: The meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with Hiḍimbā in the dreadful forest, and the birth of Ghaṭotkaca, are related right here.
t.1.2.85: The Pāṇḍavas' wandering in disguise, their dwelling in the house of a brahmin, the slaying of Baka, and the astonishment of the townspeople.
t.1.2.86: Then Arjuna, having vanquished Aṅgāraparṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā, went toward the Pāñcālas together with all his brothers.
t.1.2.87: Then the Tāpatya, the Vāsiṣṭha and the excellent tale of Aurva, and the wondrous episode of the five Indras are told right here.
t.1.2.88: Then comes Drupada's deliberation over the five having a single wife, and the superhuman marriage of Draupadī, ordained by the gods.
t.1.2.89: And the arrival of Vidura, and the sight of Keśava, the dwelling at Khāṇḍavaprastha, and likewise the rule over half the kingdom.
t.1.2.90: And at Nārada's command, the agreement concerning Draupadī was made; there too the tale of Sunda and Upasunda is recounted.
t.1.2.91: The forest-dwelling of Pārtha, and his meeting with Ulūpī on the way, the journey to the holy tīrthas, and the birth of Babhruvāhana.
t.1.2.92: And in Dvārakā the loving Subhadrā was won by the Diadem-wearer, who desired her, with the consent of Vāsudeva.
t.1.2.93: When Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had arrived bringing the bridal gifts, there followed the obtaining of the discus and the bow, and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
t.1.2.95: Thus has the first book, the Ādiparvan, been described in great detail; two hundred chapters and eighteen more were counted in it by the supreme seer Vyāsa of surpassing splendor.
t.1.2.94: The birth of Abhimanyu of supreme splendor in Subhadrā, the escape of Maya from the blazing fire and the deliverance of the serpent, and the birth of sons to the great seer Mandapāla in the Śārṅgī bird.
t.1.2.96: Seven thousand ślokas, and likewise nine hundred, and eighty-four ślokas: such is the text that was seen by the great-souled one.
t.1.2.97: The second, the Sabhāparvan, is said to be rich in events: the building of the assembly hall of the Pāṇḍavas and the appearance of the Kiṃkaras.
t.1.2.98: Then comes the account of the assembly halls of the World Guardians, told by Nārada, who had seen the gods; the beginning of the Rājasūya, and likewise the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha.
t.1.2.99: The release by Kṛṣṇa of the kings held captive in Girivraja; and likewise, at the Rājasūya, during the dispute over the guest-offering, the slaying of Śiśupāla.
t.1.2.100: And the mockery by Bhīma, on the floor of the assembly hall, of Duryodhana, who was filled with grief and indignation on seeing that splendour at the sacrifice.
t.1.2.101: There his wrath arose, because of which he had the game of dice arranged, and there the cunning gambler Śakuni defeated the son of Dharma at dice.
t.1.2.102: There, when they had sunk in the ocean of the dice game, Draupadī, like a boat, carried them across out of the ocean; learning that they had crossed over, King Duryodhana then once again challenged the Pāṇḍavas to the dice game.
t.1.2.103: All this, the Sabhāparvan, was narrated by the great-souled one. In number, seventy-two chapters are to be known here.
t.1.2.104: Two thousand ślokas, five hundred ślokas, and eleven ślokas are to be known as declared in this parvan.
t.1.2.105: After this, the third should be known as the great Āraṇyaka, and in it is the following of the citizens after the wise son of Dharma.
t.1.2.106: Where the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāñcālas came in full number, where the tale of the slaying of Saubha is told, and likewise the slaying of Kirmīra, and the sojourn away of Pārtha of boundless splendor for the sake of weapons.
t.1.2.107: Then the battle with Mahādeva, who had taken the form of a Kirāta, the sight of the Lokapālas, and the ascent to heaven.
t.1.2.108: The appearance of the great seer Bṛhadaśva, whose self was perfected, and the lament of the afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira in his misfortune.
t.1.2.109: Right here is the most righteous Tale of Nala, which gives rise to compassion, wherein is told the steadfastness of Damayantī when calamity befell Nala.
t.1.2.110: And to the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, who had gone to dwell in the forest, Lomaśa related the news of Arjuna's doings in heaven.
t.1.2.111: Likewise, the pilgrimage to the sacred fords of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas is described here, and in that very place the slaying of Jaṭāsura is also narrated.
t.1.2.112: And Bhīmasena, commissioned by Draupadī on Gandhamādana, where, for the sake of mandāra flowers, he assailed that lotus pond.
t.1.2.113: Where a very great battle took place between him and the Rākṣasas, and also the mighty Yakṣas led by Maṇimat.
t.1.2.114: And also the tale of Agastya, in which Vātāpi is devoured, and the seer's going to Lopāmudrā for the sake of offspring.
t.1.2.116: The story of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, who had been a celibate student from his youth; the story of Rāma Jāmadagnya, of abundant splendor.
t.1.2.117: Where the slaying of Kārtavīrya and of the Haihayas is described, and also the tale of Sukanyā, in which Cyavana the Bhārgava appears.
t.1.2.115: Then, right after that, comes the tale of the Hawk and the Dove, in which Indra, Agni and Dharma sought to test King Śibi.
t.1.2.119: Right here is the Tale of Jantu, in which King Somaka, for the sake of sons, offered sacrifice with his son, and he obtained a hundred sons.
t.1.2.118: Where, at the sacrifice of Śaryāti, he made the two Nāsatyas drinkers of soma, and where that sage was restored to youth by the two of them.
t.1.2.121: Having obtained the divine weapons, Savyasācin fought, for the sake of his guru, a battle with the Nivātakavacas who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura.
t.1.2.120: Right here too is the Aṣṭāvakrīya, in which the ṛṣi, having defeated Bandin in debate, regained his father, who had gone to the ocean.
t.1.2.122: And the reunion of Pārtha with his brothers on Gandhamādana, and the Ghoṣayātrā, the expedition to the cattle-stations, where Kirīṭin fought with the Gandharvas.
t.1.2.123: And then their return to the lake of Dvaitavana, and the abduction of Draupadī by Jayadratha from within the hermitage.
t.1.2.126: The tales of Sāvitrī and of Auddālaki, and also the story of Vainya, and right here too the Rāmāyaṇa episode, told at great length.
t.1.2.124: Where Bhīma, equal to the wind in swiftness, followed him; and, in the session with Mārkaṇḍeya, the tales told one after another.
t.1.2.125: Then come the visit of Kṛṣṇa and the conversation with Satyā, the tale of the measure of rice, and likewise the tale of Indradyumna.
t.1.2.127: Here is the robbing of Karṇa of his two earrings by Puraṃdara, and the Āraṇeya tale, in which Dharma instructed his son, and in which the Pāṇḍavas, having obtained boons, went toward the western direction.
t.1.2.128: This is declared to be the third book, the Āraṇyaka Parva. In it the supreme seer has counted two hundred chapters, and sixty-nine chapters more are likewise proclaimed.
t.1.2.129: Eleven thousand ślokas and six hundred, and likewise sixty-four ślokas: thus this parvan has been declared.
t.1.2.130: After this, learn this Vairāṭa, the full account of the book: having gone to the city of Virāṭa and seen a great śamī tree in the cremation ground, the Pāṇḍavas deposited their weapons there.
t.1.2.131: Where they, having entered the city, dwelt there in disguise, and where the slaying of the evil-souled Kīcaka came about at the hands of Vṛkodara.
t.1.2.132: where, at the cattle raid, the Kurus were defeated in battle by Pārtha, and where the wealth of cattle belonging to Virāṭa was set free by the Pāṇḍavas;
t.1.2.133: Where Uttarā was given by Virāṭa as daughter-in-law to Kirīṭin, intended for Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of foes.
t.1.2.136: Know next, O listener, the fifth, the Udyogaparvan: when the Pāṇḍavas had encamped at Upaplavya, Duryodhana and Arjuna, both eager for victory, approached Vāsudeva.
t.1.2.134: This extensive fourth parva, the Vairāṭa, has been described. Here too the count of the chapters has been made by the great-souled one.
t.1.2.135: There are a full sixty-seven chapters; now hear from me also the total of the ślokas: two thousand ślokas and fifty ślokas have been declared in this parvan by the supreme seer in his count.
t.1.2.137: "You ought to give the two of us your help in this battle": when these words had been spoken, there the great-minded Kṛṣṇa replied.
t.1.2.138: O bulls among men, myself as a counsellor who will not fight, or an akṣauhiṇī of troops: to which of you shall I give what?
t.1.2.139: Then the dull-souled, evil-minded Duryodhana chose the army, while Dhanaṃjaya chose Kṛṣṇa as his counsellor, who would not fight.
t.1.2.140: There the mighty great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra sent Saṃjaya as an envoy to the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of peace.
t.1.2.141: And where, having heard of the Pāṇḍavas led by Vāsudeva, Dhṛtarāṣṭra fell into sleeplessness through anxiety.
t.1.2.142: Where Vidura made the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra hear words that were varied and beneficial.
t.1.2.145: Where the greatly renowned Kṛṣṇa, moved by compassion and desiring a treaty, came himself to the city named after the elephant to make peace.
t.1.2.143: Likewise, there is the section where the king, filled with anguish of mind and absorbed in grief, was made by Sanatsujāta to hear the unsurpassed teaching on the self.
t.1.2.144: And where, at daybreak in the assembly of kings, Saṃjaya proclaimed the oneness of the mighty Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
t.1.2.147: where Kṛṣṇa, having discovered the wicked plot devised by Karṇa, Duryodhana and the others, displayed his mastery of yoga among the kings.
t.1.2.146: And the rejection by King Duryodhana of Kṛṣṇa, who, for the sake of peace, was asking for what was beneficial to both sides.
t.1.2.148: Where Karṇa, made to mount the chariot by Kṛṣṇa, was artfully counseled by him, and where Kṛṣṇa, out of Karṇa's pride, was rejected by him.
t.1.2.149: And then too came the counting of the forces, of chariots, horses, men and elephants, by the one who marched out from the city of Hāstinapura.
t.1.2.151: This, the fifth book in the Bhārata, full of very many events, is declared to be the Udyogaparva, concerned with peace and war.
t.1.2.150: Where, when the great battle was to take place on the morrow, the king, speaking cruel words through an embassy, sent Ulūka to the Pāṇḍavas; and where the reckoning of the rathas and atirathas, and also the tale of Ambā, are told.
t.1.2.153: And ninety-eight ślokas have been uttered in this parvan by the great-souled Vyāsa of noble mind, O ascetics rich in austerity.
t.1.2.152: Here, by count, the chapters are held to be one hundred and eighty-six, and of ślokas there are six thousand and just as many hundreds.
t.1.2.154: After this, they declare the Bhīṣmaparva, of wondrous content, in which Saṃjaya described the formation of Jambūkhaṇḍa.
t.1.2.155: Where a terrible, exceedingly dreadful battle took place for ten days, and where the army of Yudhiṣṭhira fell into the deepest despair.
t.1.2.157: where Pārtha of the mighty bow, placing Śikhaṇḍin in front and striking him with sharpened arrows, brought Bhīṣma down from his chariot.
t.1.2.156: Where Vāsudeva, of great wisdom, dispelled the despondency of Pārtha, born of delusion, by means of reasons that revealed liberation.
t.1.2.158: This is proclaimed as the sixth great book in the Bhārata; one hundred chapters are declared for it, and seventeen others as well.
t.1.2.159: Five thousand eight hundred and eighty-four ślokas in number are proclaimed in this parvan, the Bhīṣmaparvan, as counted by Vyāsa, the knower of the Veda.
t.1.2.160: Then is told the Droṇaparvan, wondrous and full of many events, in which the Saṃśaptakas drew Pārtha away from the field of battle.
t.1.2.162: Where many great chariot-warriors of the world, led by Jayadratha, slew Abhimanyu, a heroic boy who had not yet reached youth.
t.1.2.161: There the great king Bhagadatta, equal to Śakra in battle, was slain by Kirīṭin together with his elephant Supratīka.
t.1.2.163: Where, after Abhimanyu had been slain, the enraged Pārtha in battle slew seven akṣauhiṇīs and then King Jayadratha was killed; and the remnant of the Saṃśaptakas was utterly annihilated in the fight.
t.1.2.165: Here too, when Droṇa had been struck down in battle, Aśvatthāman, enraged, manifested the fierce Nārāyaṇa weapon.
t.1.2.164: Alambuṣa and Śrutāyu, the valiant Jalasaṃdha, Saumadatti, Virāṭa, the great chariot-warrior Drupada, and others led by Ghaṭotkaca were slain in the Droṇaparvan.
t.1.2.166: This is declared to be the seventh great parvan in the Bhārata. Here, in the Droṇaparvan, those kings, the heroes named as bulls among men, for the most part met their death.
t.1.2.167: One hundred chapters have been declared, and seventy chapters besides; likewise eight thousand ślokas and nine hundred as well.
t.1.2.169: After this is told the Karṇaparvan, most wondrous, wherein the wise king of the Madras is appointed to the charioteership, and where the ancient tale of the destruction of Tripura is recounted.
t.1.2.168: Likewise, nine ślokas have been counted here in the Droṇaparvan by the sage Pārāśarya, the seer of truth, after careful reflection.
t.1.2.170: And here, on the march, there is the harsh exchange between Karṇa and Śalya; and here too is the tale of the swan and the crow, joined with taunting.
t.1.2.171: And the anger of Yudhiṣṭhira and Kirīṭin toward one another, and where, in a single chariot combat, the great chariot-warrior Karṇa was slain by Pārtha.
t.1.2.172: This has been designated the eighth parvan by those who reflect on the Bhārata. Sixty-nine chapters are declared in the Karṇaparvan, and exactly four thousand and nine hundred ślokas.
t.1.2.173: After this is proclaimed the Śalyaparvan, of wondrous content, in which, when the army's foremost heroes had been slain, the lord of the Madras became its leader.
t.1.2.174: In the Śalyaparvan, where the chariot battles that took place are recounted one by one, the destruction of the foremost of the Kurus is related.
t.1.2.175: Here too is the death of Śalya at the hands of the Dharmarāja, the great chariot-warrior; and in this very place the tumultuous mace-fight is recounted, and the holiness of the tīrthas of the Sarasvatī is proclaimed.
t.1.2.176: This wondrous and meaningful parvan has been declared the ninth; in it, fifty-nine chapters have been counted by those skilled in enumeration.
t.1.2.177: Many events are recounted here, and the total number of ślokas is declared: three thousand two hundred and twenty ślokas, composed by the sage, concerning the Kauravas who bore glory.
t.1.2.179: When the Pārthas had gone away, those three chariot-warriors, Kṛtavarmā, Kṛpa and Drauṇi, came there at evening, smeared with blood.
t.1.2.180: Where Drauṇi, the great chariot-warrior of unyielding wrath, vowed: "Without slaying all the Pāñcālas led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the Pāṇḍavas together with their counselors, I shall not take off my armor."
t.1.2.178: After this I shall relate the dreadful Sauptika Parvan, in which the implacable King Duryodhana, his thighs broken, was found.
t.1.2.181: Where those bulls among men, led by Drauṇi, slew the Pāñcālas together with their retinues as they lay asleep at night, trusting and unsuspecting.
t.1.2.183: Where Draupadī, stricken with grief for her sons and tormented by the slaughter of her father and brothers, resolved to fast unto death and sat down before her husbands.
t.1.2.182: There the five Pārthas were saved by relying on the strength of Kṛṣṇa, and so was Sātyaki, the great archer, while all the rest met their death.
t.1.2.184: Where, at Draupadī's word, Bhīma of terrible prowess, enraged, ran after Bhāradvāja, the son of his guru.
t.1.2.185: There, out of fear of Bhīmasena and urged on by fate, Drauṇi in his fury released his weapon with the words, "For the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas!"
t.1.2.187: The curses laid upon one another by Drauṇi, Dvaipāyana and the others; and the water rite for all the kings, in the section on the offering of water.
t.1.2.186: "Not so!" said Kṛṣṇa, countering those words of his; and there Phālguna quelled that weapon with a weapon of his own.
t.1.2.188: And the account of Karṇa, secretly born of Pṛthā as her own son, is also told here; this is the tenth book, the Sauptika.
t.1.2.189: In this parvan the great-souled one has recited eighteen chapters, and the number of ślokas here is likewise declared to be eight hundred.
t.1.2.191: After this, they declare, comes the Strīparva, which gives rise to compassion, wherein is recorded the exceedingly pitiful lament of the heroes' wives, and the fit of anger and the subsequent forgiveness of Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.2.190: And seventy ślokas, by exact count, were declared by the one of boundless intellect in the book that joins the Sauptika and the Aiṣīka.
t.1.2.192: where they beheld those heroic kṣatriyas, who had met their destined end and never turned back, their sons, brothers and fathers, slain in battle.
t.1.2.193: where the king, greatly wise and foremost among all upholders of dharma, had the bodies of those kings burned in accordance with the scriptures.
t.1.2.194: This is declared to be the eleventh book, great and exceedingly sorrowful; twenty-seven chapters are recited in this book.
t.1.2.196: After this comes the Śāntiparvan, the twelfth, which increases understanding, wherein Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmarāja, fell into despondency after having caused the slaying of his fathers, brothers, sons, kinsmen and relatives.
t.1.2.195: Seven hundred and seventy-five ślokas are said to be counted here. For here the Bhārata narrative, composed by the great-souled author, sets flowing tears of anguish from the hearts of good people.
t.1.2.197: And in the Śāntiparvan are expounded the dharmas taught from the bed of arrows, which ought to be properly understood by kings who seek knowledge of statecraft.
t.1.2.198: There too are the duties for times of distress, which reveal the causes of the times, and by rightly understanding them a man may attain all-knowledge; and the duties of liberation are also told, varied and greatly extended.
t.1.2.199: This is declared to be the twelfth parvan, dear to wise people. In this parvan, O you whose wealth is austerity, three hundred chapters are to be known, and likewise thirty-nine chapters more.
t.1.2.201: After this, know the excellent Ānuśāsana, in which Yudhiṣṭhira, king of the Kurus, returned to his natural state after hearing the settled conclusions on dharma from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhāgīrathī.
t.1.2.200: Fourteen thousand ślokas are proclaimed, and they say five hundred more as well, together with twenty-five in number.
t.1.2.202: Here the conduct that serves dharma and artha is set forth in its entirety, and also the manifold ways in which the various kinds of gifts bear their fruits.
t.1.2.203: Likewise, the distinctions among worthy recipients, the highest rule of gifts, the application of the rules of conduct, and the supreme course of truth.
t.1.2.204: This is the excellent Anuśāsana, abounding in very many narratives; and right here Bhīṣma's attainment of heaven is recounted.
t.1.2.205: This is the thirteenth parva, which brings about certainty concerning dharma; in it there are one hundred and forty-six chapters, and of ślokas there are six thousand and seven hundred.
t.1.2.206: Then the fourteenth parvan, called the Āśvamedhika, is declared; in it is the unsurpassed tale of Saṃvarta and Marutta.
t.1.2.207: The acquisition of the golden treasure is told, and the birth of Parikṣit, who, having earlier been burned by the fire of the weapon, was brought back to life again by Kṛṣṇa.
t.1.2.208: As the Pāṇḍava followed the horse that had been released to roam at will, there were battles here and there with impetuous, unforgiving princes.
t.1.2.210: Thus has this most wondrous Āśvamedhika Parvan been told. In it one hundred and thirty-three chapters are declared.
t.1.2.209: And here Dhanaṃjaya was brought into mortal peril in battle by Babhruvāha, the son of Citrāṅgadā, the appointed daughter. And at the great sacrifice, the Aśvamedha, there is also the tale of the mongoose.
t.1.2.211: Three thousand ślokas, and as many hundreds, and twenty ślokas as well, have been counted by the seer of truth.
t.1.2.213: Seeing him set out, the virtuous Pṛthā too followed him then, abandoning her sons' kingdom, devoted to serving her elders.
t.1.2.214: Wherein the king saw his slain sons, grandsons and other kings, heroes who had gone to the other world, come back again.
t.1.2.212: Then comes the parvan called Āśramavāsa, known as the fifteenth, in which the king, having given up the kingdom, set out together with Gāndhārī, and Vidura too went to the hermitage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.2.216: Where Vidura, having taken refuge in dharma, attained the blessed goal, as did Saṃjaya, the wise and self-controlled minister, son of Gavalgaṇa.
t.1.2.217: There Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, saw Nārada, and from Nārada he heard of the great slaughter of the Vṛṣṇis.
t.1.2.218: This is the very great and wondrous Parvan called Āśramavāsa, described before; this Parvan, by enumeration, contains forty-two chapters.
t.1.2.215: Having seen, through the grace of the seer Kṛṣṇa, a wonder beyond compare, he cast off his grief and, together with his wife, attained the supreme perfection.
t.1.2.219: One thousand ślokas, and five hundred ślokas, and likewise six ślokas more have been counted by the seer of truth.
t.1.2.220: After this, learn of this dreadful Mausala Parvan, in which those tigers among men, who in battle could endure the touch of weapons, were crushed by the staff of a brahmin's curse near the salt sea.
t.1.2.221: At a drinking party, overcome by drink and driven on by fate, they struck one another down with thunderbolts that had taken the form of erakā grass.
t.1.2.223: Where Arjuna, that bull among men, having come to Dvāravatī and seen it bereft of the Vṛṣṇis, fell into despondency and the deepest anguish.
t.1.2.222: There, having brought about the destruction of all, those two, Rāma and Keśava, did not escape Time when it arrived, Time that takes away everything and is the same for all.
t.1.2.224: Having paid honor to Śauri, the best of the Yadus and his own maternal uncle, he beheld the great slaughter of the Yadu heroes at the drinking-place.
t.1.2.226: Then, having taken with him the people of Dvāravatī, the old and the young, he witnessed, in that grievous calamity, the defeat of the Gāṇḍīva.
t.1.2.225: He had the funeral rites performed for the body of Vāsudeva and of the great-souled Rāma, and for the Vṛṣṇis in order of their rank.
t.1.2.227: and the unresponsiveness of all the divine weapons, the destruction of the wives of the Vṛṣṇis, and the impermanence of powers.
t.1.2.229: Thus has this Mausala Parvan, the sixteenth, been proclaimed; eight chapters are declared in it, and three hundred ślokas.
t.1.2.228: Having seen this, he fell into despair; then, urged on by Vyāsa's words, he approached Dharmarāja and commended renunciation to him.
t.1.2.230: After that, the Mahāprasthānika is known as the seventeenth book, in which the Pāṇḍavas, bulls among men, having renounced their kingdom, went together with the queen Draupadī to the supreme perfection.
t.1.2.231: Here three chapters have been declared, and likewise one hundred and twenty ślokas have been counted by the seer of truth.
t.1.2.232: Next is to be known the Svargaparvan, which is divine and beyond the human. In this parvan five chapters have been counted by enumeration, and two hundred ślokas have been reckoned, O you whose wealth is austerity.
t.1.2.233: Thus these eighteen books have been declared in full. In the supplements, the Harivaṃśa and the Bhaviṣya are also proclaimed.
t.1.2.234: Thus the whole Bhārata has been told by way of the summary of its books. Eighteen akṣauhiṇīs assembled with the desire to fight, and that great and terrible battle lasted eighteen days.
t.1.2.236: But once one has heard this tale, nothing else worth hearing gives delight, just as the crow's voice sounds harsh once one has heard the cry of the male cuckoo.
t.1.2.235: A clever twice-born who knows the Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads, but does not know this tale, would by no means be truly wise.
t.1.2.237: From this supreme history arise the inspirations of poets, just as the arrangements of the three worlds arise from the five elements.
t.1.2.238: O twice-born ones, the Purāṇa abides within the domain of this narrative, just as the four kinds of creatures abide within the domain of the sky.
t.1.2.240: No tale exists on earth that does not rest upon this narrative, just as the sustaining of the body is not possible without relying on food.
t.1.2.239: This tale is the support of all the virtues of action, just as the manifold workings of the mind are the support of all the senses.
t.1.2.241: This tale is drawn upon for their livelihood by all the finest poets, just as a nobly born lord is depended upon by servants who seek their own advancement.
t.1.2.242: He who takes in the Bhārata as it is recited, immeasurable, meritorious, purifying, sin-destroying and auspicious, issued forth from the lips of Dvaipāyana, what need has he of bathing in the waters of Puṣkara?
t.1.2.243: This great and unsurpassed tale, rich in meaning, has here been laid out by way of a summary of its books; having heard it at the outset, men find it easy to plunge into, just as the vast salt ocean becomes easy to enter by means of a boat.
